paras: The lynching of P. A. Rymer was the hanging of a U.S. Army soldier from Fort Lyon, Colorado, by a masked mob that took him from the jail at West Las Animas on the night of August 20, 1882. Rymer was accused of having stabbed a fellow soldier, William McGarvey, to death two nights earlier. Wire reports said the mob of forty or fifty men was supposed to be soldiers from the fort, and the story ran across the country under headlines such as "Lynched by Soldiers" and "Military Hanging."

According to a special to the Denver Republican from Las Animas, Rymer and McGarvey, both soldiers stationed at Fort Lyon, quarreled over a bottle of whisky on the night of August 18. The dispatch said Rymer "stabbed and instantly killed McGarvey with a pocket knife" and added that there was "strong talk of lynching Rymer by the other soldiers." Rymer was held in the jail at West Las Animas. None of the reports gives the race of either man.

A Denver dispatch of August 22 reported that on the night of the 20th Rymer was taken from the jail and hanged by "a mob of forty or fifty masked men, supposed to be soldiers from the fort." The Dodge City Times printed a fuller account gathered from a traveler who had passed through Las Animas on Monday. In that version about fifty soldiers from the fort demanded the prisoner, and when the deputy sheriff in charge refused, their leader ordered them to fire into the jail windows although the deputy's family lived in the rooms upstairs. The soldiers then overpowered the deputy, broke in the jail door with a bar of railroad iron, took Rymer out and hanged him.
The reports do not say where Rymer was hanged, though an Omaha Bee headline described him as "Braced Up on a Beam by a Masked Mob."

The Denver dispatch said that Major Brayton, commanding at Fort Lyon, was "exercising all diligence in his power to ferret out who composed the mob," and called the lynching the "second chapter" of the killing, with "the end not yet." No report of arrests, an inquest, a court-martial or any result of the investigation appears in the coverage.

The story reached readers as a short Associated Press-style wire item dated Denver, August 22, which ran in more than a dozen papers from Maine to Washington Territory between August 22 and early September. Before the hanging, the Republican's report of the stabbing had circulated in western papers, already predicting a lynching by the soldiers. Headlines stressed the military identity of the lynchers: "Lynched by Soldiers" in Lancaster, "Military Hanging" in Seattle, "Murderer Lynched by Soldiers" in Burlington, and "A Blue Coat Murderer Hanged" in Montana's Benton Weekly Record.

Several papers headlined the item simply as lynch law, with "Judge Lynch in Colorado" in the Sacramento Record-Union and "The Usual End" in the St. Paul Globe, and placed it beside reports of other lynchings and expected lynchings that week. The wire copy called Rymer a "murderer" without qualification and offered no editorial comment on the mob, while the Dodge City Times called the episode a "Horrible Affair."

Accounts differ on the first killing and its timing: the Denver reports said Rymer stabbed McGarvey on Friday night, while the Dodge City traveler said both drunken soldiers fired and one dropped dead on Monday morning, with the lynching following the same day. Most papers put the mob at forty or fifty men, but the Lancaster Intelligencer printed "forty-eight or fifty" and the Rock Island Argus "four hundred and fifty," apparently a garbling of the same wire figure. The Dillon Tribune dated the hanging to August 22, the date of the Denver dispatch rather than of the event.

accounts.label: Denver wire report
accounts.gist: Rymer, who stabbed McGarvey near Fort Lyon on Friday, was taken from the West Las Animas jail on the night of the 20th and hanged by forty or fifty masked men supposed to be soldiers; Major Brayton was investigating.

accounts.label: Traveler's account (Dodge City Times)
accounts.gist: After a drunken exchange of shots Monday morning, about fifty soldiers demanded the prisoner, fired into the jail windows, overpowered the deputy sheriff, broke the door with railroad iron and hanged him.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Denver wire verbatim under headlines such as 'Hanged by a Mob', 'Lynch Law' and 'The Usual End'.
Headlines emphasized soldiers as lynchers: 'Lynched by Soldiers', 'Military Hanging', 'United States Soldiers Lynch a Comrade for Murder'.
The Dodge City Times called it a 'Horrible Affair' while calling Rymer 'the murderer'.

conflicts.note: The Denver reports derive from a Las Animas special written the next day; the Dodge City version is second-hand from a traveler.
Aug. 22 is the dispatch date; the wire's 'night of the 20th' is the most specific.
The Lancaster and Rock Island figures look like garbles of the wire's 'forty or fifty'.

No paper gives the race of Rymer or McGarvey; both are identified only as soldiers at Fort Lyon.
Forty or fifty masked men supposed to be soldiers from Fort Lyon.
A mob of soldiers that besieged the jail; no organized band named.
